ideas.title: Don't Run to Him
ideas.premise: When my brother broke through the ice by the creek mouth at sunset, I was forty meters away with only my phone and the ice picks around my neck, and he had about ten minutes of useful strength left.
ideas.hook: If your brother falls through the ice, don't run to him.
ideas.twist: Everyone's instinct is to sprint to the hole and grab them, which loads the same weak ice and often puts a second person in the water. The red dashed 'mistake' ghost shows that run cracking the ice. The safe order is: call 911, stay back, get down flat and slide on your stomach to spread your weight, reach or throw something (Eli slides his ice picks across on their cord) instead of going yourself, tell him to kick flat and pull out, and both of you roll away along the path he came in on.
ideas.world: Eli narrates, first person, past tense. The SIDE view at sunset shows the brother's red shack, the creek mouth and the crack opening. The 'mistake' ghost run happens under the blue 'paused' freeze-frame, then a white flash rewinds to the correct version. The TOP map shows the runner's path as a red arrow and the safe slide as a green one. The CUT view shows the brother with his arms on the ice. Blue hour arrives as he rolls free. The brother distance pill shrinks slowly while Eli slides flat. Ends on the 'PART 2' card (what happens in the hour after).
diagrams: TOP map: the red dashed straight-line sprint vs. a slow flat slide, with brother distance pill counting down
911-call card with three things to say: lake, landmark (red shack), 'person in water'
Callout comparing standing (all weight on two boot prints) vs. lying flat (weight spread out)
Swatch chips as steps: STEP 1 CALL · STEP 2 REACH / THROW · STEP 3 DON'T GO
1-10-1 phase strip running on the brother's in-water timer
ideas.fact: Minnesota DNR rescue guidance for someone who has fallen through: call 911, then reach or throw something to them rather than going out yourself. The 1-10-1 principle (about 1 minute of cold shock, 10 minutes of useful movement, up to 1 hour before passing out from hypothermia) is published by the National Center for Cold Water Safety, based on Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht's research.
ideas.verify: The exact Minnesota DNR wording and step order ('reach, throw, go' or similar) for helping someone who fell through. Whether official guidance supports tossing your own ice picks to the person. The 1-10-1 numbers and their source. Any claim that rescuers become victims needs a named source and number before it goes in, or it gets cut.
ideas.risk: Medium. Rescue advice must stay exactly within official guidance (no going into the water, no improvised tricks). The pack has no rope, so the reach/throw object has to be Eli's ice picks on their existing neck cord, or a plain callout line. The user's topic already fits the frozen lake, so nothing had to move. It shows a family member in danger: keep it calm, no gore, and he gets out.

ideas.title: The Hour After
ideas.premise: A sequel to 'Ten Minutes Under': I had just pulled myself out of the creek-mouth hole, soaked, at blue hour, with about an hour before the cold would knock me out and my brother's red shack two hundred meters away.
ideas.hook: You have one hour after you climb out of the ice.
ideas.twist: The myth is that once you're out you're safe, so you stand up, walk it off and rub your arms and legs warm. The safe actions: stay low and roll or crawl away from the hole along your own footprints, don't stand until the ice is thicker, get to shelter, get the wet layers off and dry layers on, call 911, and warm the body gently. Don't rub the arms and legs.
ideas.world: Eli narrates. Opens on the CUT view freeze-frame from the last episode, then a whip-zoom to the SIDE view of him lying and rolling. The TOP map shows his footprint trail back to the brother's red shack. The December clock runs from 4:40 at blue hour into night. The in-water timer turns into a 'since out' timer. The brother runs in and calls 911. Snow starts.
diagrams: 1-10-1 card with the last '1' (one hour) highlighted, now on a 'since out' timer
TOP map: back along your own footprints to the red shack, with a red ghost path straight across the creek ice
Callout on Eli lying flat: 'Roll first, stand later'
Swatch chips: WET OFF · DRY ON · CALL 911 · KEEP WARM
Water-temperature pill swapping to an air-temperature reading
ideas.fact: The 1-10-1 principle's 'one hour' before passing out from hypothermia, published by the National Center for Cold Water Safety (from Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht). Advice to handle a cold person gently, remove wet clothing and not rub the arms and legs comes from Mayo Clinic / American Red Cross hypothermia first aid.
ideas.verify: The 1-10-1 figures. The exact hypothermia first-aid wording from Mayo Clinic, the American Red Cross or the CDC (no drinks, no medicines, no doses). Whether 'roll away and crawl back along your own path' matches Minnesota DNR self-rescue guidance.
ideas.risk: Medium. It touches first aid, so it must stick to basic official steps: no medicines, no drinks, no heating devices. There is no shack interior art, so warming up happens at the shack door or is only narrated. A direct sequel is allowed.

ideas.title: Footprints Aren't Proof
ideas.premise: At sunset, I followed my brother's morning footprints straight toward his red shack, sure the ice had held him, and I had about ten minutes of light left before the trail ran out at the creek mouth.
ideas.hook: Why you must never trust footprints on a frozen lake.
ideas.twist: The myth: if someone already walked here, it's safe. Footprints only show that the ice held earlier, under someone else's weight. Sun, current at a creek mouth and snow cover change it. White, snowy ice is weaker than clear ice. The safe action: check the thickness yourself as you go, stay away from creek mouths and moving water, wear ice picks, and turn back. This time Eli stops before the crack. He doesn't fall in.
ideas.world: Eli narrates, at sunset into blue hour. Opens on the boot-print close-up (his brother's prints, with Eli's boots stepping into them). The SIDE view follows the footprint trail toward the creek mouth. The CUT view ruler shows the ice getting thinner under the same trail, with the current moving below. The TOP map lays the trail over the creek. The ice-thickness pill drops step by step. The brother waves from his red shack. Freeze-frame on the hole that's about to crack, then Eli backs away.
diagrams: Boot-print close-up with a tag: 'Held HIM, this MORNING'
CUT cross-section: thickness ruler along the trail, getting thinner over the current
Minnesota DNR ice-thickness ladder card (walking line highlighted)
Swatch chips: CLEAR ICE vs WHITE ICE with a strength note
TOP map: footprint trail running across the creek mouth, with a safe route arrow around it
ideas.fact: Minnesota DNR ice guidance: at least about 10 cm (4 inches) of new clear ice to walk on; white or snow ice is roughly half as strong, so double the thickness; ice near moving water such as creek mouths is often thinner; 'no ice is ever 100% safe'.
ideas.verify: The DNR walking thickness in centimeters and the exact wording of the white-ice 'half as strong / double it' guidance. The DNR's warning about inlets and current. That the DNR ladder card in the pack matches the current published numbers.
ideas.risk: Low to medium. It's close to 'Ten Minutes Under' (thin ice over the creek), so make it a near-miss with no fall, and focus on footprints as a false proof. Any check-the-ice tool (spud bar) has no art, so the CUT ruler does that job.

ideas.title: Keep the Jacket On
ideas.premise: When the ice dropped me in by the creek, my first panicked thought was to pull off my heavy winter jacket so it wouldn't drag me down, with one minute of gasping and ten minutes of strength to decide.
ideas.hook: If you fall through the ice, don't take off your jacket.
ideas.twist: The myth: heavy wet winter clothes pull you under, so strip them off. In reality, air trapped in a winter jacket helps you float at first and keeps some warmth in. The safe actions: keep it on, control your breathing through the first minute of cold shock, turn back toward the ice you came from, arms on the ice, kick flat, then roll away.
ideas.world: Eli narrates. The CUT cross-section is the star: trapped air glowing inside the orange jacket, the current below, the thickness ruler. The red dashed mistake ghost unzips and loses its air bubbles under a blue freeze-frame. The SIDE view at blue hour shows him with arms on the ice and kicking flat. His brother calls from the red shack. The brother distance pill closes in. The in-water timer and 1-10-1 strip run throughout.
diagrams: CUT view callout: 'trapped air = floats you' on the jacket, then the ghost version without it
1-10-1 phase strip, the first '1' marked 'BREATHE, don't strip'
Angle meter: kick flat, body close to horizontal
Swatch chips: KEEP IT ON · BREATHE · TURN BACK · KICK FLAT
In-water timer next to the water-temperature pill
ideas.fact: The National Center for Cold Water Safety advises keeping winter clothing on in cold water because trapped air helps you float and the layers slow heat loss; its 1-10-1 principle comes from Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht's research.
ideas.verify: The exact NCCWS (or another recognized source's) guidance on keeping clothes on and on trapped air. Don't make claims about how long the jacket keeps you afloat without a source. The 1-10-1 figures.
ideas.risk: Medium. It overlaps a lot with 'Ten Minutes Under' (another self-rescue with 1-10-1), so the jacket myth has to carry the whole episode. It could be told as a sequel with the brother falling in, but he has no name or voice yet.

ideas.title: Fifty Meters, No Shore
ideas.premise: At night, a snow squall caught me halfway between my brother's red shack and the shore, I couldn't see the pines or the shacks, and every step I took 'straight for shore' bent me toward the thin creek ice.
ideas.hook: If snow catches you on the ice, don't walk for shore.
ideas.twist: The myth: just walk in a straight line and you'll hit shore. Without landmarks, people drift into curves and even circles, and here that curve leads to the creek mouth. The safe actions: if a whiteout comes, stay in or next to the shack, call your partner or 911, use your phone's map or compass, or go back exactly along your own fresh footprints, and check the forecast before going out.
ideas.world: Eli narrates, first in blue hour and then at night with heavy snow on the SIDE view. The TOP map shows the runner's path curving toward the creek mouth as a red dashed ghost arc. The brother distance pill grows as Eli drifts away. The December clock runs into night. The boot-print close-up shows his own prints filling in with snow. A white flash, then he turns back to the red shack.
diagrams: TOP map: the 'straight' line he meant to walk vs. the curve he actually walked, ending at the creek mouth
Brother distance pill growing while Eli thinks he's getting closer to shore
Boot-print close-up with prints filling in with snow, tagged 'your way back'
Swatch chips: STAY · CALL · MAP · BACKTRACK
Ice-thickness pill dropping as the curve reaches the creek
ideas.fact: A 2009 study in Current Biology by the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics (Souman et al.) found that people walking without visual landmarks drift off course and often walk in circles. The National Weather Service issues Snow Squall Warnings for sudden whiteouts.
ideas.verify: The study's details and that it fairly supports the claim that people walk in circles without landmarks. It wasn't done on ice, so the narration must not overstate it. What the National Weather Service says about snow squalls. Any official ice-safety guidance on whiteouts (Minnesota DNR) for the 'stay put' advice.
ideas.risk: Medium. The key fact comes from a study done off the ice, and the pack has no compass or phone map art (show it with callouts and the TOP map). Heavy snow has to stay readable at phone size.
